column21:
🧭 Periportal Lesion

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis.
📌 Summary
  • Periportal abnormality is a pattern, not a single diagnosis: the differential spans edema/fluid, dilated ducts, thrombosed or collateral vessels, cysts, infiltrative tumor, fibrosis, gas, stones, and calcified arteries.
  • Periportal edema surrounds the portal triad/portal venous branch; a dilated bile duct typically courses along one side of the accompanying portal vein. Edema and ductal dilation may coexist.
  • Nonenhancing thrombosed portal branches can mimic dilated ducts, while cavernous transformation creates enhancing or Doppler-positive periportal collateral channels.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
Ultrasound / Doppler
  • Ascending cholangitis: circumferential duct-wall thickening with echogenic debris/sludge and/or choledocholithiasis; Doppler helps separate avascular ducts from adjacent vessels.
  • Cavernous transformation: tortuous periportal collateral vessels with flow; long-standing portal-vein thrombosis may leave no identifiable normal portal vein.
  • Portosystemic collateral routes include intrahepatic portal-to-hepatic venous shunts and recanalized paraumbilical veins.
  • Acute viral hepatitis: starry-sky portal-triad echogenicity and gallbladder-wall edema; periportal edema may also be visible on CT/MR.
  • Focal fatty sparing: focal hypoechoic liver region within an echogenic fatty liver, crossed by undisplaced vessels and without mass effect; common near the gallbladder and segment IV.
  • Pneumobilia: central branching echogenic foci with reverberation/dirty shadowing; portal venous gas extends more peripherally.
  • Peribiliary cysts: small cystic structures adjacent to portal triads that do not communicate with the biliary tree; CT/MR lesions may parallel portal veins and mimic ducts.
  • Hepatic schistosomiasis: echogenic periportal fibrotic mantle/clay-pipestem fibrosis, with possible bull's-eye or mosaic appearance.
  • Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis: intrahepatic stones/sludge in dilated ducts, periductal inflammatory echogenicity, and no intraductal Doppler flow.
CT / MR / Cholangiography
  • Hypervolemia can produce a low-density periportal collar with a distended IVC; passive congestion adds enlarged hepatic veins/IVC and venous reflux.
  • MRCP/direct cholangiography depicts ductal anatomy and helps distinguish branching ducts from edema, cysts, fibrosis, or thrombosed portal branches.
  • PSC produces multifocal irregular strictures and dilated segments with a beaded ductal appearance; AIDS cholangiopathy can mimic this pattern and more typically includes papillary/distal CBD stenosis.
  • Recent liver transplant may normally show periportal edema. In contrast, biliary necrosis, indistinct ducts, and bilomas should raise concern for hepatic-artery stenosis or thrombosis.
  • Malignancy may obstruct ducts or encase vessels. Enhancing portal-vein tumor thrombus favors malignant invasion; inflammatory pseudotumor can closely mimic cholangiocarcinoma.

⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Do not equate every post-trauma periportal collar with blood: focal laceration/hematoma supports hemorrhage, whereas a distended IVC and systemic volume expansion support resuscitation-related lymphedema.
  • Do not call every periportal low-attenuation branch a bile duct; thrombosed portal branches, edema, peribiliary cysts, fibrosis, and perivascular steatosis are important mimics.
  • Do not interpret isolated periportal edema after liver transplant as allograft injury; expected postoperative lymphatic disruption can produce this appearance.

⭐ Super Summary
  • First decide whether the periportal structure is fluid/edema, duct, vessel/collateral, cyst, tumor, fibrosis, gas, stone, or calcified artery; then use Doppler flow, contrast enhancement, ductal communication, distribution around the portal vein, and clinical context to resolve the mimic.

column11: Why can hepatic-artery stenosis or thrombosis cause biliary necrosis and intrahepatic bilomas after liver transplantation?

When the hepatic artery is severely stenosed or thrombosed, ischemic injury can affect the biliary tree before diffuse hepatic infarction develops. Duct walls become indistinct or necrotic and bile can leak into intrahepatic collections, producing bilomas. Imaging consequence: biliary necrosis, irregular/dilated ducts, and bilomas in a liver allograft should trigger assessment of hepatic arterial patency.
